The pond loach (Misgurnus anguillicaudatus) reaches a maximum recorded total length of 28 centimeters [Li = 28 centimeters], making it one of the larger members of the cobitid family. This ultimate size is attained after several years of steady growth, with the most rapid increases occurring during the juvenile phase. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae, following chorion rupture, have an extremely modest mass at birth of approximately 0.001 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.001 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of the related species Misgurnus fossilis. These lecithotrophic larvae depend entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days post-hatching, and their small starting mass places them among the more diminutive freshwater teleost hatchlings known from temperate Asian water bodies. The transition to exogenous feeding begins once the yolk sac is fully resorbed, and at that stage the developing fish must locate suitable micro-prey items in the benthic zone, a challenge that imposes high early-life mortality under natural conditions.

Sexual maturation in Misgurnus anguillicaudatus begins when individuals attain a total length of approximately 11 centimeters [Lp = approximately 11 centimeters], a size threshold that signals the onset of gonadal recrudescence and gametogenesis. This length at puberty corresponds to a body mass of roughly 7.88 grams [Wwp = roughly 7.88 grams], estimated from the length-weight relationship specific to the species. Achieving this developmental milestone typically requires several seasons of successful foraging in productive habitats. Reproductively active adults become gravid during the spring spawning period, and females can be identified by their visibly distended abdomens filled with vitellogenic oocytes. The ability to reproduce at this relatively modest size is an adaptation to unpredictable environments, as it ensures that at least some individuals contribute to the next generation even if they fail to reach the maximum possible dimensions. Field surveys indicate that the smallest sexually mature individuals are often found in marginal habitats where growing conditions are suboptimal.

At a total length of 23 centimeters, a size commonly recorded among the largest pond loach in well-established populations, the reproductive output under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 16 °C [T = 16 °C] reaches approximately 2000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 2000 eggs per year]. This annual egg production represents the maximum fecundity rate observed for the species, expressed as the total number of oocytes released per year by a single gravid female during the peak of the spawning season. The strong dependency of reproductive rate on body size is a well-documented pattern in iteroparous freshwater fish, with larger females contributing disproportionately more offspring to the population. The temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C] used in these experiments reflects the optimal thermal regime for ovarian development and oviposition in this species, which is native to cool-temperate streams and rice paddies. At lower temperatures, gametogenesis slows considerably; at higher temperatures, metabolic demands may reduce the energy available for egg production.

The asymptotic body mass of the pond loach, representing the theoretical maximum wet weight an individual can achieve over its lifetime, is estimated at 136 grams [Wwi = 136 grams]. This ultimate wet weight corresponds to the 28-centimeter maximum length and is typical for a benthic-feeding cobitid inhabiting nutrient-rich lowland waters. Comparisons with related species show that Misgurnus anguillicaudatus attains a slightly larger maximum mass than its congener Misgurnus fossilis, a difference likely linked to its more extensive geographic range and greater access to productive habitats. The growth trajectory toward this asymptotic mass decelerates markedly after puberty, as energy is increasingly diverted toward reproductive effort. Seasonal variations in food availability, particularly during the winter months when metabolic rates decline, cause periodic plateaus in weight gain. Field studies using mark-recapture methods have confirmed that few individuals in wild populations ever reach this maximum size, highlighting the strong influence of environmental constraints on lifetime growth.

Maximum longevity in Misgurnus anguillicaudatus, based on observations of the closely related Misgurnus fossilis, is estimated at approximately 7300 days [am = approximately 7300 days] when maintained under stable environmental conditions with a water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This extended lifespan is notable for a small-bodied freshwater fish and reflects a slow pace of life that includes deferred reproduction and prolonged somatic investment. In the wild, few individuals are likely to attain this theoretical maximum age due to predation pressure from piscivorous birds and larger fish, as well as habitat disturbance from agricultural practices. The same thermal regime of 16 °C [T = 16 °C] that supports optimal reproductive rates also appears to minimize age-related physiological deterioration, effectively decelerating the onset of senescence. Comparative analyses within the Cobitidae suggest that the pond loach's longevity is tied to its ability to enter a state of metabolic suppression during unfavorable periods, a strategy that reduces cumulative oxidative damage and extends the functional lifespan beyond what body size alone would predict.
